question: Which statement best describes any: opting out of the type system?
options: never is the type with no values. A function that never returns (throws or loops forever) returns never, and an empty union is never. It's also what a fully narrowed variable becomes when every case has been eliminated — the basis for exhaustiveness checks.

Both accept any value, but they differ on the way out. any lets you use the value freely (unsafe); unknown forces you to prove its type first (safe). Prefer unknown at boundaries (API responses, parsing, catch clauses) and only reach for any as a last-resort escape hatch.

unknown can hold any value, just like any, but it flips the safety rule: you can't do anything with an unknown until you narrow it (with typeof, instanceof, or a type guard). It's the correct type for values whose shape you don't know yet, like JSON.parse results or caught errors.

any tells the compiler 'stop checking this value.' Anything is assignable to any and any is assignable to anything, so you lose all safety: property access, method calls, and arithmetic are all allowed even when they're wrong. It's contagious — once a value is any, expressions derived from it are any too.
